correctness.rationale: For every N>=6 congruent 2 mod4, the exact polygonal gauge is the max over supporting facet functionals at apothem cos(pi/N); 2024 theorem 2.13 reduces the global James max to a vertex and its unique isosceles unit partner. The vertical partner is the top edge midpoint (0,cos(pi/N)). Direction atan(cos(pi/N)) lies strictly between pi/4-pi/(2N) and pi/4, selecting the asserted nearest odd-multiple facet normal in each modulo-eight class. Substitution gives the two closed formulas; Taylor series gives signs of the cubic corrections. Running the embedded standard-library program from the staged file location verified fourteen values, 448 sampled local profiles, and two known exact special cases; infinite quantification is proved analytically, not numerically.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The new claim is two exact closed values for every N=4m+2 plus a residue-dependent third-order asymptotic. The general vertex theorem reduces maximization to a vertex but gives no prescribed maximizing facet and therefore no direct n-formula; the proof supplies the strict side-dependent closest-normal comparison. The general Radon bound J<=3/2 cannot recover precise values, and the Birkhoff-restricted invariant does not imply the classical one. Stronger coverage may nonetheless reside in the inaccessible 2020 paper, so no absolute novelty claim is made.

value.rationale: The classical James constant is a standard sharp quantitative measure of nonsquareness; polygonal Radon planes are a canonical, infinite and independently motivated structural class. The result classifies the invariant for every member rather than sampling isolated polygons, identifies a strict modulo-eight switch of the maximizing facet, and gives nontrivial opposite third-order terms even though both branches tend to the Hilbert value. Values J(X6) and J(X10) are known checks, not the motivation or sole asserted novelty. The exact natural family and asymptotic parity law make the computation potentially reusable, without claiming a downstream theorem or arbitrary parameter gain.
